title: War and Drought Are Choking the World's Most Vital Trade Routes
excerpt: From the Strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea and Black Sea, simultaneous disruptions at critical maritime chokepoints are driving up shipping costs and threatening global energy and food security.
body:
• The Strait of Hormuz, which carried 25% of the world's seaborne oil before the Iran war began in February 2026, has seen daily vessel traffic plummet from 130-140 ships to fewer than a dozen.
  • Brent crude hit $126 per barrel at its peak, the largest monthly oil price increase ever recorded, with prices still volatile around $83-89 as Iran-Oman negotiations stall.
  • Red Sea and Black Sea disruptions have compounded the crisis, with Houthi attacks and Ukraine-Russia strikes forcing costly rerouting around the Cape of Good Hope.
  • Global losses from these combined disruptions are estimated at $10.7 billion per year in delays and rerouting, plus $3.4 billion in elevated freight costs.

The global shipping network is under siege on multiple fronts. The Strait of Hormuz remains largely blocked nearly six months after the United States and Israel launched airstrikes against Iran on February 28. The Red Sea continues to be contested by Houthi forces. The Black Sea has become more dangerous as Ukraine and Russia intensify strikes on each other's shipping infrastructure. And the Panama Canal, though recovering, still carries the scars of drought-induced restrictions.

Never in modern history have so many critical maritime chokepoints been disrupted simultaneously.

Hormuz: The World's Most Important Bottleneck

The Strait of Hormuz is just 34 kilometers wide at its narrowest point, yet before the crisis, roughly 20 million barrels of oil and 20% of the world's liquefied natural gas passed through it daily. The waterway connects Persian Gulf producers — Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Iraq, and Qatar — to the rest of the world. In 2024, 84% of crude oil shipments through the strait went to Asian markets, with China receiving a third of its oil via this route.

Since Iran closed the strait in early March 2026, vessel traffic has collapsed. Shipping data shows daily transits have fallen from an average of 130-140 vessels to as few as four to six on some days in August. The International Maritime Organization reported in April that about 20,000 mariners and 2,000 ships were stranded in the Persian Gulf.

"The Strait of Hormuz will remain closed as long as the U.S. does not change its behavior and accept Iran's conditions to end the war."

— Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, August 2026

Oil prices tell the story. Brent crude surged past $100 per barrel on March 8 for the first time in four years, peaking at $126 — the largest single-month price increase in the history of the oil market, according to industry data. Prices have since retreated to the $83-89 range as markets price in partial reopening hopes, but negotiations between Iran and Oman over control of the strait remain fraught.

Red Sea and Black Sea: Compounding the Pressure

The Hormuz crisis does not exist in isolation. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have continued attacking commercial vessels in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb strait, the passage linking the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean. Ship tonnage through the Suez Canal and Gulf of Aden dropped by over 70% during the most intense periods of conflict.

Vessels forced to bypass the Suez Canal and travel around the Cape of Good Hope add 10 to 14 days to standard journeys between Europe and Asia. Container shipping rates from China to Northern Europe surged 248% from November 2023 levels during earlier Red Sea disruptions, and the latest escalation is pushing costs higher again.

In the Black Sea, a surge in attacks on ships, ports, and export terminals has turned yet another waterway into a strategic chokepoint. Russia and Ukraine have intensified strikes on each other's agricultural export facilities and commercial vessels, disrupting exports of oil and grain that many countries depend on.

India's Exposure

India is particularly vulnerable to these overlapping disruptions. The country is the world's third-largest oil consumer and imports roughly 85% of its crude. A significant share of India's energy imports — including oil from Iraq and LNG from Qatar — normally transit the Strait of Hormuz. Indian refiners have sought to load crude at Iraq's Basrah Oil Terminal at steep discounts, but shipowners remain wary of entering the waterway, according to Reuters.

The human toll has touched India directly. An Indian crew member was killed and eight others wounded when Iranian cruise missiles struck two Emirati oil tankers during the conflict. The Indian-flagged cargo ship Haji Ali sank in May after an attack in the strait, and the tanker Sanmar Herald was among vessels targeted.

The crisis has also disrupted fertilizer supply chains critical to Indian agriculture. Up to 30% of internationally traded fertilizers normally transit the Strait of Hormuz, with the Persian Gulf region accounting for roughly a third of global urea exports.

The Price Everyone Pays

Quantitative studies cited by UNCTAD estimate combined global losses of $10.7 billion per year in delays and rerouting, plus an additional $3.4 billion annually in elevated freight costs. War-risk insurance premiums — which for large tankers increased from 0.125% to up to 0.4% of ship value per transit at the start of the conflict — feed directly into consumer prices for fuel, food, and manufactured goods.

"The world has built its trading system on the assumption that international sea lanes will remain open even during periods of political tension. That assumption is becoming increasingly fragile."

— The Business Standard

What to Watch

Iran and Oman are negotiating a framework to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, with Iran seeking fees of 5% to 7% of cargo value for transit and Oman proposing around 3%. The United States wants no fees. Meanwhile, the US has said it could maintain a naval blockade of Iran indefinitely. With Brent crude still swinging several dollars on each headline, the markets are signaling that resolution remains far from certain — and that every shipment of oil, grain, and fertilizer sailing a longer route is adding to the cost of goods worldwide.
nri_angle: India is highly exposed as a major oil importer dependent on Hormuz transit, with Indian crew members killed in attacks and fertilizer supply chains for Indian agriculture disrupted.
